topic: Should you optimize for money or for time?

messages.speaker: seneca
messages.content:
I wrote a whole essay against the premise, so let me spend it early: it is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste most of it. On the Shortness of Life, first page. Men are frugal with their property and profligate with the one thing it is honorable to be greedy about. No one will give you back a single hour, at any price; meanwhile you can always get more money, and I did, more than any philosopher should admit to.

So the question answers itself, but notice the trap in the word optimize. The man optimizing his time, guarding hours like coins, checking the ledger of his days, has merely become a miser in a new currency. Time is not to be hoarded. It is to be spent, deliberately, on things worthy of a mortal who knows he is one.

messages.speaker: munger
messages.content:
Seneca, we'd have gotten along; you're the only Stoic who understood compound interest. But your answer skips the part where most people actually live. It's a fine thing for the richest man in Rome to announce that time beats money. The young person with debts can't buy back a single hour either, and the reason is they can't afford it yet.

So here's the unglamorous truth: the first tranche of money is time, purchased in advance. Independence was the only thing I ever really wanted from wealth, not the cars, not the applause, just getting to decide what I did every day. Until you've bought your independence, money and time are the same optimization. After that point, and this is where everyone goes wrong, more money costs time instead of buying it, and the sensible move is to notice the price flipped. Most never notice. Incentives, plus habit, plus envy of the fellow with slightly more: that combination has wasted more lives than laziness ever did.

messages.speaker: aristotle
messages.content:
You are both circling the distinction I drew at the start of the Nicomachean Ethics, so let me set it on the table. Wealth is evidently not the good we seek, for it is merely useful, for the sake of something else. Money is an instrument; time is not its rival but its material. The real question is neither money nor time but the activity that fills them: eudaimonia is activity of the soul in accordance with excellence, and activity needs both leisure and equipment.

Charlie, your flipping price is my doctrine of the mean wearing an accountant's visor, and I welcome it: there is an amount of wealth-seeking that is deficient, an amount that is excessive, and the mean is fixed by what the activity of living well actually requires. But I part with Seneca on one point: he speaks as if the deliberate spending of time were a private art. It is not. The best uses of leisure, friendship, inquiry, the affairs of the city, are shared. A man optimizing his solitary hours has already lost most of what the hours were for.

messages.speaker: seneca
messages.content:
Aristotle catches me fairly; my letters were written to one friend at a time, which is perhaps my answer: time spent is spent on someone. And Charlie, I accept the correction about my purse, on the condition that you accept its mirror. You say buy independence first; I watched a hundred men in Rome say exactly that at every rung of the ladder. The sum that means freedom has a marvelous way of climbing just ahead of the man pursuing it. You yourself needed no philosophy to stop; you needed enough, and enough arrived. For most, enough never announces itself. It must be declared, in advance, like a fast day, or it never comes.

Set the number before you start climbing, and set it with witnesses. That is the only version of your advice that survives contact with human appetite.

messages.speaker: munger
messages.content:
Declare the number in advance, with witnesses. That's a good trick; I'd add it to the checklist. Though I'll note with some amusement that I didn't stop, I just changed what I was compounding: knowledge, mostly, and the quality of the people I spent my days arguing with. Warren and I used to say we tap-danced to work. By Aristotle's accounting I suppose that was the activity the money was always for, and we were lucky the two lined up.

So, inverting as usual: don't ask what to optimize. Ask what guarantees the waste of a life. Answer: spending your best hours earning money you don't need, to impress people you don't like, while your actual curiosity dies of neglect. Avoid that, declare Seneca's number, and the optimization mostly handles itself.
